catalog_quote: The Kwomtari language does not exhibit contrasts in nasalisation, tone or vowel length. The only suprasegmental worthy of discussion in this section is stress. Stress is difficult to hear; often syllables seem to carry equal stress, or a given word is pronounced with different stress on different occasions. There are no examples of contrastive stress. In a bisyllabic word uttered in isolation, the first syllable often sounds stronger, but the second syllable carries rising pitch. As noted in §2.2, a syllable containing schwa is not stressed (with the single exception of /mənə/ [ˈmənə]), so a word containing schwa in its initial syllable will normally have its stress on the second syllable. ... audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quotation confirmed verbatim in the Drew 2008 text we hold at the stated locators (section 5 pp. 42-43; section 2.2 p. 29), and the OPD 2004 contra-quote also confirmed verbatim. (2) The classification rests on the only phonological description of the language, a 2008 SIL phonology sketch with an explicit suprasegmentals section and frame elicitation; Glottolog's full descriptive bibliography is this single volume, and web search found nothing newer or instrumental (only Baron 1983 survey, downloaded, silent). (3) No unheld work would improve the record; list of works to obtain empty. (4) Coding 'variable' (no contrastive stress, inconsistent placement, phrase-final prominence in frames, schwa unstressable) faithfully reflects Drew's own hedged conclusion; the earlier OPD 'lexical' reading is superseded by the later, fuller analysis from the same SIL programme. Status well-sourced; no action.
